verses.text: There was a man in the land of Uz, whose name was Job. That man was blameless and upright, and one who feared God,  and turned away from evil.
There were born to him seven sons and three daughters.

His possessions also were seven thousand sheep, three thousand camels, five hundred yoke of oxen, five hundred female donkeys, and a very great household; so that this man was the greatest of all the children of the east.
His sons went and held a feast in the house of each one on his birthday; and they sent and called for their three sisters to eat and to drink with them.

It was so, when the days of their feasting had run their course, that Job sent and sanctified them, and rose up early in the morning, and offered burnt offerings according to the number of them all. For Job said, “It may be that my sons have sinned, and renounced God in their hearts.” Job did so continually.
Now on the day when God’s sons came to present themselves before Yahweh,  Satan also came among them.
Yahweh said to Satan, “Where have you come from?” Then Satan answered Yahweh, and said, “From going back and forth in the earth, and from walking up and down in it.”
Yahweh said to Satan, “Have you considered my servant, Job? For there is no one like him in the earth, a blameless and an upright man, one who fears God, and turns away from evil.”
Then Satan answered Yahweh, and said, “Does Job fear God for nothing?
Haven’t you made a hedge around him, and around his house, and around all that he has, on every side? You have blessed the work of his hands, and his substance is increased in the land.
But stretch out your hand now, and touch all that he has, and he will renounce you to your face.”
Yahweh said to Satan, “Behold,  all that he has is in your power. Only on himself don’t stretch out your hand.” So Satan went out from the presence of Yahweh.
It fell on a day when his sons and his daughters were eating and drinking wine in their oldest brother’s house,
that there came a messenger to Job, and said, “The oxen were plowing, and the donkeys feeding beside them,
and the Sabeans attacked, and took them away. Yes, they have killed the servants with the edge of the sword, and I alone have escaped to tell you.”

While he was still speaking, there also came another, and said, “The fire of God has fallen from the sky, and has burned up the sheep and the servants, and consumed them, and I alone have escaped to tell you.”

While he was still speaking, there came also another, and said, “The Chaldeans made three bands, and swept down on the camels, and have taken them away, yes, and killed the servants with the edge of the sword; and I alone have escaped to tell you.”
While he was still speaking, there came also another, and said, “Your sons and your daughters were eating and drinking wine in their oldest brother’s house,
and behold, there came a great wind from the wilderness, and struck the four corners of the house, and it fell on the young men, and they are dead. I alone have escaped to tell you.”
Then Job arose, and tore his robe, and shaved his head, and fell down on the ground, and worshiped.
He said, “Naked I came out of my mother’s womb, and naked shall I return there. Yahweh gave, and Yahweh has taken away. Blessed be Yahweh’s name.”
In all this, Job did not sin, nor charge God with wrongdoing.

footnotes.content: A man in Uz: we meet Job—blameless, upright, one who feared God. The old stories tell us fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom, and here we see what it looks like lived out: a man who doesn't just talk about faith, but turns away from evil day by day.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Seven sons and three daughters—a full quiver. In those days, children were both a sign of blessing and the measure of a man's hope for the future. Job had much to live for, much woven into his heart.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Seven thousand sheep, three thousand camels, five hundred yoke of oxen, five hundred donkeys, and a great household—the numbers tell you what prosperity looked like. Job was the greatest of all the children of the east, not just wealthy but preeminent. Yet all this will become the testing ground.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: His sons held feasts in each one's house on his birthday, and called their sisters to join them. You see families together, celebrating their bond, unaware that everything is about to change. How little we know of what waits beyond the next day.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: When the days of feasting were over, Job would rise early and offer burnt offerings for each of his children, saying, 'It may be my sons have sinned and cursed God in their hearts.' Job did this continually—a father's constant intercession, his priestly watch over his children's souls. This is the love that fears the Lord more than comfort.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The day when God's sons came to present themselves before Yahweh, and Satan came among them. The veil is drawn back, and we see what we cannot usually see: the unseen realm where heaven's courts gather, and rebellion walks in with them.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Yahweh asks Satan where he has been. Satan's answer—going back and forth in the earth, walking up and down in it—shows a restless malice, prowling, ever vigilant, looking for what he can undo. Yet he speaks before Yahweh, under the gaze of the Almighty.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Yahweh asks Satan, 'Have you considered my servant, Job? There is no one like him in the earth—a blameless and upright man who fears God and turns from evil.' The Lord himself brings Job into Satan's gaze, lifts him up for notice. This is the moment the trial begins.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Satan's taunt is sharp: 'Does Job fear God for nothing?' He strikes at the heart of the question that will echo through the whole book—is faith real only when it's rewarded? Can a man love God just because God is God?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Satan protests that Yahweh has hedged Job around—his house, all he has—and blessed the work of his hands until his substance increases in the land. Satan sees the fence, and his jealousy reads it as an easy shelter that keeps Job safe from real choosing.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: 'Stretch out your hand and touch all that he has, and he will renounce you to your face,' Satan says. The challenge is set: remove the blessing, and faith will crumble. Strip away the comfort, and love will turn to curse.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Yahweh said to Satan, 'Behold, all that he has is in your power. Only on himself don't stretch out your hand.' And Satan went out from the presence of Yahweh. The boundary is set: Job's life is protected, but everything else falls into Satan's reach. The trial is granted.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: It fell on a day when his sons and daughters were eating and drinking wine in their oldest brother's house. A normal day, a family gathered. No warning. No shadow falls across the feast.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: There came a messenger to Job: 'The oxen were plowing, and the donkeys feeding beside them.' The work of the land, tending the flocks—the rhythm of a blessed life, unbroken, until the words that follow.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Sabeans attacked and took them away; they killed the servants with the edge of the sword. Only the messenger escaped. The first loss comes swiftly—livestock and hired hands, gone in one stroke. The news bearer's voice carries only his own escape.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: While he was still speaking, another came and said, 'The fire of God has fallen from the sky and burned up the sheep and the servants.' One messenger before the last has finished, the next brings worse news. The pile of loss grows faster than Job can absorb it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: There came another: 'The Chaldeans made three bands and swept down on the camels and killed the servants.' The camel herds—his wealth—taken. Again, only the messenger lives. The attacks pile on, each one a different hand, each one decisive.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: While he was still speaking, there came also another: 'Your sons and your daughters were eating and drinking wine in their oldest brother's house.' The words begin to name what matters most, what cannot be replaced.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A great wind from the wilderness struck the four corners of the house, and it fell on the young men, and they are dead. The house collapsed. All ten children—his seven sons and three daughters—are gone in a moment. The final messenger arrives with the unbearable news.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Then Job arose, and tore his robe, and shaved his head, and fell down on the ground, and worshiped. Here is the raw expression of grief—the tearing, the shaving, the collapse—but then: worship. In the ash of everything, his first movement is toward the God who allowed it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: 'Naked I came out of my mother's womb, and naked shall I return there. Yahweh gave, and Yahweh has taken away. Blessed be Yahweh's name.' These words cut to the bone: Job sees that all he held was a gift, borrowed, never his to keep. And still he blesses the One who gave and took. This is the faith Satan wagered could not stand.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: In all this, Job did not sin, nor charge God with wrongdoing. Readers today hear an echo in Job's silence: how many times have we felt the weight of loss and felt the temptation to name God as cruel? Yet here, in the rubble of his own life, Job will not take that easier path. His refusal speaks across the centuries.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
